red.focus: Distinguish legal authority from evidence about outcomes
red.summary: Law tells institutions what rules they may apply, while empirical research can show how those rules work. Learn why a useful study is not automatically binding law and why a binding law is not automatically effective policy.
checklist: I can identify the governing legal source
I can distinguish empirical evidence from normative authority
I can ask what outcomes a rule is intended to change

sections.title: Rules and Results Answer Different Questions
sections.body_md: A city law requires safety inspections. The statute tells officials what they must do; a study may show whether inspections reduce accidents. Both matter, but they have different roles. A positive legal source establishes authority, while empirical data helps assess outcomes. An expert report does not repeal legislation because its findings are persuasive. Equally, the fact that a rule is legally valid does not establish that it achieves its objective. Good legal reasoning keeps those questions separate.

An expert report does not repeal legislation because its findings are persuasive. Equally, the fact that a rule is legally valid does not establish that it achieves its objective. Good legal reasoning keeps those questions separate.

sections.title: Start With an Observable Claim
sections.body_md: A politician says a new penalty makes streets safer. That is an empirical claim: we should look for changes in injury, behavior, enforcement and other possible explanations. A lawyer must also identify what the penalty actually authorizes and whom it affects. A study could show that one measure fails, yet the lawful decision about changing it may belong to a legislature. Understanding law's social world means knowing what evidence can establish and what only a competent institution may decide.

sections.title: Ask Whose Outcomes Count
sections.body_md: A rule could lower reported offenses but increase unlawful detention or administrative burdens. Measuring success therefore requires defining more than one outcome. The analyst should consider affected people, costs, benefits, unintended effects and which outcomes the law itself prioritizes. Numbers do not choose our values for us. They reveal consequences that decision makers must evaluate with legal and ethical reasons. This distinction is foundational to responsible economic and empirical study of law.

yellow.focus: Evaluate evidence used to justify legal rules
yellow.summary: Learn to distinguish descriptive data, causal estimates and normative goals in legislative or judicial arguments. Identify who collected evidence, what it measures and whether it supports the proposed decision.
checklist: I can separate correlation from an effect claim
I can identify relevant source and measurement limits
I can explain why evidence quality affects policy justification

sections.title: A Trend Is Not Yet an Effect
sections.body_md: Road deaths fall after a new traffic penalty. That is evidence of a change, but it does not prove the penalty caused the decline. Weather, vehicle technology, travel volume and enforcement practices could also matter. A careful analyst compares the observed data with a credible account of what would have happened without the change. The distinction between description and causation is essential when government asserts that restricting liberty will solve a public problem.

A careful analyst compares the observed data with a credible account of what would have happened without the change. The distinction between description and causation is essential when government asserts that restricting liberty will solve a public problem.

sections.title: Measurement Can Hide the Problem
sections.body_md: If a city measures public safety only through reported crimes, changes in reporting practices may create a misleading trend. A new hotline could increase reports even as underlying harm decreases. Data must be interpreted through definitions, collection methods, missing cases and incentives to report. The analyst should ask which measure best reflects the protected interest and whether groups experience different outcomes. Numbers can make policy clearer only when the meaning of the numbers is understood.

sections.title: Evidence Is Part of Reason-Giving
sections.body_md: Some legal decisions require factual justification under constitutional, administrative or statutory standards. Other choices are largely legislative policy judgments. A lawyer must identify the institution's legal duty to give reasons, then assess whether the evidence actually supports its conclusion. A well-designed empirical analysis can expose an unsupported assumption, but it cannot substitute for the governing legal standard. Sound advocacy links lawful authority, reliable evidence and a transparent explanation.

orange.focus: Analyze institutional evidence under economic incentives
orange.summary: Compare the legal force of different decisions with the incentives and information influencing their evidence. Understand why measurement can change behavior when it becomes a target.
checklist: I can identify incentive-driven measurement distortions
I can compare observational and experimental evidence
I can evaluate institutional competence in policy choice

sections.title: People Respond to How Success Is Measured
sections.body_md: A court administration may reward faster case closure. Judges and staff might then reduce delays, but some cases could be closed without adequate attention. A metric can alter the behavior it seeks to measure. The analyst should examine whether quality, review, error rates and affected-person experience changed alongside speed. An institution may lawfully use performance metrics while still needing safeguards against manipulation. A single headline number rarely captures justice.

sections.title: Experiments and Comparisons
sections.body_md: An experimental study randomly assigns a permissible intervention, making causal comparison easier when conditions are met. Many legal policies cannot be randomized ethically or practically, so analysts use observational designs and carefully chosen comparison groups. Both approaches require attention to selection, measurement, spillovers and external validity. A lawyer should ask whether the evidence really supports the expected policy effect in the population the law will govern. This avoids treating statistical authority as equivalent to legal or moral authority.

sections.title: Who Should Decide?
sections.body_md: Courts may have power to assess evidence in a particular case but limited capacity to design and monitor an entire regulatory system. Legislatures and agencies may gather broader evidence yet face political and administrative incentives. A sophisticated analysis identifies the lawful allocation of authority and what information each institution can reliably evaluate. Evidence can reveal errors in policy, but the choice of remedy or reform must remain tied to the institution's actual mandate and the rights of those affected.

black.summary: At doctoral depth, evaluate the role of social science in legal legitimacy while preserving the distinction between facts, values and lawful institutions. Defend accountable use of evidence under uncertainty.
checklist: I can distinguish empirical efficiency from rights justification
I can evaluate expertise and democratic accountability
I can design audit mechanisms for evidence-driven governance

sections.title: Evidence Cannot Choose the Constitution
sections.body_md: A rigorous study might show that intrusive surveillance reduces one class of offenses. It does not by itself establish that the surveillance is legally permissible or morally justified. Rights, equality, privacy and institutional limits impose independent constraints. A doctoral theory of evidence-based governance should distinguish causal findings from the decision rule governing their use. Treating statistical improvement as conclusive authority risks replacing public law with unaccountable technocratic preference.

A doctoral theory of evidence-based governance should distinguish causal findings from the decision rule governing their use. Treating statistical improvement as conclusive authority risks replacing public law with unaccountable technocratic preference.

sections.title: Experts Also Make Choices
sections.body_md: Researchers choose outcomes, samples, comparison groups and models. Those choices can be technically defensible but reflect which harms or populations receive attention. A serious legal scholar should examine preregistration, replication, data access, uncertainty and the people excluded from the study. Expertise deserves respect because of method and evidence, not simply institutional prestige. Public decisions relying on science should explain why a particular estimate is relevant and how its limitations were considered.

sections.title: Accountability in Policy Learning
sections.body_md: Imagine a regulation justified by a disputed forecast. A principled design could specify measurable objectives, independent evaluation, protected rights, sunset review and a transparent process for correcting harmful effects. Each safeguard must fit the governing constitutional and administrative framework. The goal is not to wait for perfect certainty before acting, nor to make evidence immune from challenge. It is to create institutions that learn from facts while remaining answerable to the human beings they govern.
